lead: Two voices speak to tired people today. Isaiah tells the exiles that the God who calls the stars by name never grows weary and gives his strength to the faint. In the Gospel Jesus says, “Come to me, all you that are weary”. The psalm, “Bless the Lord, O my soul”, gives thanks for the God who forgives and heals. What the prophet promised, Jesus now offers in person.

r.h: He does not faint or grow weary
set: Isaiah 40–55, the Book of Consolation, speaks to the Jews in exile in Babylon in the years before Cyrus let them go home (539 BC). They are surrounded by great temples and by the worship of the stars, and they feel forgotten. This passage answers their complaint.
str: vv. 25–26: God has no equal; he brings out the stars like an army and calls each by name.
vv. 28–31: God never tires, and he gives strength to those who wait for him.
kw: God’s otherness: nothing in creation can be compared with him. Yet in v. 29 the Holy One bends down to the faint.
To wait with eager hope. The POC translates “those who trust in God”, which brings out the same attitude from another side.
vv: Why do you say, O Jacob, and speak, O Israel, “My way is hidden from the Lord, and my right is disregarded by my God”?
God takes up the people’s complaint in their own words before he answers it. An honest complaint is a beginning of prayer.
He gives power to the faint, and strengthens the powerless.
but those who wait for the Lord shall renew their strength, they shall mount up with wings like eagles, they shall run and not be weary, they shall walk and not faint.
The line goes from flying to running to walking. The strength of God is given most of all for the long and ordinary walk.
ch: The Catechism says that hope responds to the longing for happiness God has put in every heart, and keeps us from discouragement (CCC 1818). The Church reads these chapters throughout Advent because the people still waiting are ourselves. The God who brought the exiles home is the God who comes to us in his Son.

set: These three verses are found only in Matthew. Jesus has just spoken of unbelieving towns and has thanked the Father for revealing himself to “infants” (11:20–27). Now he turns to all who are worn out. The words sound like the invitation to Wisdom in Sirach 51:23–27, where the teacher calls people to come near and to put their necks under her yoke.
str: v. 28: the invitation and the promise of rest.
v. 29: take my yoke, learn from me.
v. 30: the reason: my yoke is easy.
kw: The wooden frame that joins oxen for work. Jewish teachers spoke of the yoke of the Law. Jesus does not offer an idle life. He offers a yoke, but it is his.
The same word as “the meek” of the Beatitudes (5:5). The one who teaches has the same gentle heart he asks of us.
It also means kind, good, well suited. A well-made yoke fits the ox and does not gall it.
vv: “Come to me, all you that are weary and are carrying heavy burdens, and I will give you rest.
The “all” has no conditions. The rest he promises is anapausis, refreshment, and it is a gift from him: “I will give”.
Take my yoke upon you, and learn from me; for I am gentle and humble in heart, and you will find rest for your souls.
“Rest for your souls” echoes Jeremiah 6:16. A disciple (mathētēs) is one who learns, and here the lesson is Jesus’ own heart.
For my yoke is easy, and my burden is light.”
ch: The Catechism quotes “Take my yoke upon you, and learn from me” when it teaches that the Word became flesh to be our model of holiness (CCC 459). Matthew’s readers would hear that Jesus speaks as God’s Wisdom in person. What Advent promises is not only that God will lift our burden, but that he will walk under it with us.

qa: How can Jesus call his yoke easy, when he also tells us to take up the cross?
The demand is real (16:24). The difference is that we do not carry it alone or by our own strength. Love makes heavy things bearable, and he is the one who walks beside us.
study: Isaiah 40:27 gives the people’s complaint in their own words. What would my own complaint to God sound like today?
What burden am I carrying alone that I could bring to Jesus at Mass today?
